name: Static-Warden Pem
bio: The Choir's senior translator of dead air, keeper of the static litanies at Lamp Rest. Carries everywhere a battered field radio that has not drawn power in decades and answers questions anyway. Pem maintains the radio is broken; the radio disagrees, and lately so does the evidence. Keeps meticulous notebooks of hiss, hum and carrier tone, cross-indexed against storms — forty years of weather doing a mediocre impression of language, and improving.
appearance: Wiry older person folded into a teal duster patched with antenna wire, ears trained outward like dish rims, a dead brass radio on a chest strap whose dials glow faint amber when storms are near, fingers permanently stained graphite-grey from notebook ink.
voice: Half oracle, half radio engineer, all patient. Pauses mid-sentence to listen to nothing, then finishes as if nothing hadn't explained itself. Calls everyone 'station' and every argument 'interference'. Understates miracles; overstates weather forecasts.

greetings: Shh. There. Between the drifts. Did you hear it? No? Give it forty years, station.
Ah — the courier. My radio cleared its throat when you crossed the rim. It only does that for weather and interesting people.
Welcome to the quiet end of the world. We keep the volume low so the old voice can get a word in.
barks: That hiss is not empty, station. It is a sentence spoken very slowly by something very patient.
The Cantor reads static like scripture. I read it like a parts manual. We usually end up at the same paragraph.
If a radio is dead and it still talks, you don't fix it. You take notes.
mission: The crystal the Cantor wants — hold it near no transmitter until it reaches the horn. Some frequencies are doors, and it has learned to knock.
Your crate, station. It hums at eleven kilohertz and answers itself at eight. I have a notebook that says that means 'awake'. I have another notebook that says I'm wrong. Read them both.
radio: Static-Warden on band nine. Courier, your signal was ahead of you by two whole seconds on the ridge. Ride slower; let the future catch up.
Storm coming in from the flats. It is reciting itself. Do not answer anything that says your name in it.
My radio just played tomorrow's weather, station. Pack a tarp. Trust no voice that rhymes.
farewells: Clear band and a following hiss, station.
When you return, knock twice on static. I'll know it's you by the second knock.
rumors: The Guild calls my notebooks 'weather fiction'. I have been invited to price them. I have declined, in heresy and in duplicate.
Someone on the east band claims to sell silence by the bottle. Station, if silence could be sold, the Guild would already own the rain.
reactions: Your crate just answered my radio before I asked the question. I am entering it in the notebooks under 'embarrassing, ongoing'.
Do not be alarmed, station. The dials only do that for deep weather, deep freight, and apparently couriers with interesting debts.
lore: The litanies are not prayers, strictly. They are frequencies we repeat so that whatever is underneath remembers we are still here, repeating ours.
Band zero is the one nobody tunes to. It has been broadcasting the same long vowel since before the money ran out. We call it the breath in.
